The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They approached Islam with hesitation and anxiety because they wanted to protect their privileges and interests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their concern grew when they understood that Islam aimed to break through the closed structure of tribal unity and replace it with a broader community.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Inside this larger community, the chiefs would lose their absolute authority over their tribes. They would now have to submit to a higher power that came from outside the narrow world of the tribe itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For this reason, many tribes delayed submitting to Islam until the movement had become the victorious political power after the conquest of Mecca.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The delegations that traveled to Mecca in the “Year of Delegations” to announce submission, obedience, and acceptance of Islam therefore seem to have been responding mainly to the new balance of power.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were accepting a reality they could no longer avoid, or they feared that the growing power of Islam would sweep over them if they continued to resist.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In general, this means that the Islam of these tribes—or, more precisely, the Islam of their chiefs—had weak foundations from the beginning.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In some cases, submission was simply a way of dealing with the stronger power and avoiding conflict with it.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In others, the chiefs were attracted by the booty Muslims gained in war and distributed among the fighters.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
All this applies mainly to the Bedouin tribes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But there was another group in the peninsula whose position was different: the settled populations of Yemen and al-Yamāma.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These people lived under stable agricultural conditions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

For that reason, they were more strongly attached to their traditions, their settled way of life, and their own religious beliefs. Their outlook was more firmly connected with the conditions in which they lived.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were therefore more resistant to change and less attracted to new ways of life.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
There was another difference as well.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Unlike Bedouin tribes, they did not have the same powerful incentive to seek war booty. Doing so would have required them to leave their settled life, migrate, and take part in military campaigns.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
A third factor was the presence of people claiming prophethood in these settled regions: Bahrain, Ḥaḍramawt, Oman, and al-Yamāma.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These were local figures who claimed to be prophets.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One was Musaylima in al-Yamāma, known in Islamic tradition as “Musaylima the Liar.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Another was a woman from the Banū Taghlib tribe named Sajāḥ, who also claimed to be a prophet. Both played a part in the Ridda Wars.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Musaylima had considerable personal influence in al-Yamāma.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Before the rise of Islam, he seems to have represented the Ḥanīf religion in that region, and there appears to have been some contact between him and Muhammad before Muhammad publicly began the Islamic mission.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Musaylima succeeded in bringing a large part of the population of al-Yamāma under his influence.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During the Ridda Wars he led what, in his own region, amounted to a counterrevolution against Islam. Muslims therefore called him “Musaylima the Liar” because of his claim to prophethood.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muslim historians say that he tried to imitate the Qur’an by producing rhymed speech in something like the Qur’anic style.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But it is not certain that the words they attribute to him are really his.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The texts preserved by these historians often sound so much like nonsense that serious historical research has good reason to doubt that they came from a prominent Arab leader of that period.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Musaylima had enough standing among his people to organize a powerful resistance to Islam that continued into the reign of Abū Bakr. He even defeated the caliph’s armies twice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The resistance was finally crushed only after Abū Bakr sent a large army under Khālid ibn al-Walīd.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Khālid defeated the movement and killed Musaylima, but his army lost many fighters from both the Anṣār and the Muhājirūn in the process.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
After this, the people of al-Yamāma were brought under Islamic authority.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Yemen came under Islamic rule during the Ridda Wars under different circumstances.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the time, its people were heavily occupied with resisting Persian rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The local leader of this resistance, another man who claimed prophethood, was killed at night in his room by his wife. She was the daughter of the Persian governor, whom he had killed before forcing her to marry him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These conditions made it easier for the Islamic army to defeat those in Yemen who had rebelled against Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Afterward, Yemen came under Islamic authority without further resistance.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Ridda movement continued to occupy much of the attention of the first two caliphs, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the second caliph, ʿUmar, used skillful political methods to bring it to a final end.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He negotiated peacefully with the chiefs of rebellious tribes and used force only when negotiation failed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In practice, the areas that resisted most strongly were the agricultural regions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This is why Banū Ḥanīfa in al-Yamāma, the region of Musaylima, were the last to submit to the caliph’s authority by force.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Defeating this storm of rebellion became one of the decisive developments that allowed the Arabs to move beyond the Arabian Peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were now able to begin a huge historical process.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Its result was not only the creation of a state and then a vast empire.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One of its greatest consequences, made possible by the rise of that state and empire, was the birth of a civilization that became a major force in social, political, and cultural history.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This historical process is what we call the Arab-Islamic conquests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
C — The Arab-Islamic Wars of Conquest
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
When the Prophet died, Islam as a political system had not yet moved beyond the borders of the Arabian Peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As a religious message and belief, however, it had already reached some neighboring countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Prophet had sent several delegations to kings and rulers, especially the kings of Persia and Abyssinia, inviting them to accept Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These missions were peaceful. They presented the basic beliefs of Islam and some of its general social principles.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
None of the rulers accepted the invitation. The king of Abyssinia was the only one who received the Arab Prophet’s delegation with warmth and friendship.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the Prophet was already preparing the way for Islam to move beyond its Arabian setting and enter the wider world.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the autumn of 629 CE, he sent a military expedition to Syria that became known as the expedition of Muʾta.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was led by Zayd ibn Ḥāritha and consisted of three thousand fighters.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This was intended as the first military encounter between the Islamic army and the Roman forces that then controlled Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

But the expedition withdrew and returned to Medina under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd after its commanders were killed one after another: Zayd ibn Ḥāritha, Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib—known as Jaʿfar al-Ṭayyār—and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Muslim force was simply not strong enough to face an army that was incomparably superior in both numbers and equipment.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This happened before the conquest of Mecca.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
After that conquest ended in a historic victory, followed by victory at Ḥunayn and the defeat of al-Ṭāʾif, the Prophet returned to the idea of confronting the Romans in Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Then came the expedition of Tabūk in the ninth year after the Hijra, 630 CE.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This time the Prophet himself led the Muslim army.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was the height of summer, and the heat was severe. The Islamic army also lacked enough money to support a long war against the Roman forces.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The expedition returned from Tabūk without fighting the Byzantines.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Even so, it achieved two important things.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
First, it gave the Muslims useful experience and helped prepare them psychologically for the wars of conquest that would follow.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Second, during the expedition the Prophet made peace agreements with the inhabitants of some of the oases along the road to Syria. This made the route safer for future Muslim armies.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
A third attempt to prepare for expansion took place during the Prophet’s lifetime.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Prophet gave Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha command of a military unit that was also to march toward Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the force had barely assembled outside Medina to prepare for departure when the Prophet became ill with the sickness that caused his death.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
When news of his death spread, the Companions hesitated.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Should the expedition continue as the Prophet had ordered, or should it be delayed?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The first Rightly Guided Caliph, Abū Bakr, decided that it should continue in order to carry out the Prophet’s wishes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In practice, the expedition rode among the tribes of Quḍāʿa, attacked Balal on the approaches to Syria in the land of Jordan, took some booty, and returned safely to Medina after being away for forty days.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It is therefore accurate to say that Islam did not move beyond the Arabian Peninsula during the Prophet’s lifetime.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But these three attempts prepared the way.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The time had now come for the movement of conquest to begin.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Two events delayed it for a while: the Prophet’s death and the outbreak of the Ridda Wars.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab-Islamic conquests beyond the peninsula began decisively during the reign of the second Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the autumn of 633 CE, shortly before ʿUmar became caliph, the armies of conquest had already begun moving through the Syrian desert toward Syria and Palestine.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were organized into three divisions, each containing 7,500 fighters.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the first year of ʿUmar’s caliphate, 634 CE, the first truly decisive battle in Arab history took place: the Battle of al-Qādisiyya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was fought west of the city of Najaf, around eighteen miles west of Kufa, in the region where the Arab state of al-Ḥīra had once stood.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Al-Ḥīra had been one of the centers of Persian control over Mesopotamia, or Iraq. Its rulers were the Arab Lakhmids, known as al-Manādhira, who were subjects of the Persian Empire.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab victory at al-Qādisiyya opened the way to the conquest of all Iraq and the final removal of Persian rule from Mesopotamia.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Between 635 and 638, the conquest of Syria and Iraq was completed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The victories of the Arab armies continued.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By the end of the ten years in which ʿUmar held the caliphate, Syria, Egypt, Palestine, Iraq, and a large part of Persia had come under Arab-Islamic rule.
